one_liner: Header-only C++20 coroutine RPC over raw TCP; its 2019 C++11 version beat brpc 1.2-1.9x on same-machine echo.
what_it_does: A server exposes ordinary free or member functions (plain or asio::awaitable-returning) with `server.register_handler<func>()`, and a client calls them with `co_await client.call<func>(args...)`, needing only the function's declaration; there is no IDL and no code generation. Arguments and results go through yalantinglibs struct_pack by default, and you can plug in your own codec through ADL `serialize`/`deserialize` overloads. It also has topic publish/subscribe and delayed responses from another thread via `rpc_context`. It is not wire-compatible with brpc or gRPC, so adopting it means replacing both ends.
how_it_is_fast: The wire format is a fixed 32-byte binary header (magic, message type, 32-bit function id, sequence number, body length) plus the body, sent with one scatter-gather `async_write`. Function ids are compile-time 32-bit MD5 hashes of the function name, dispatched through an `unordered_map`. A single `std::string_view` argument or return value skips serialization and copying, and receive buffers grow without zero-fill (`resize_and_overwrite`, or a std::string private-member hack on older libraries). The server runs one asio `io_context` per thread with one C++20 coroutine per connection and TCP_NODELAY on by default. All of this describes current master; the 2019 benchmark ran the older C++11/msgpack code.
when_to_use: Both client and server are C++20 code you own, and you want to turn existing functions into RPCs without .proto files, codegen or a build step.
Trusted-LAN or same-host links that move large strings or blobs, where passing `std::string_view` avoids serialization and copies (the README says multi-GB payloads are sent this way).
Internal tools, test harnesses or device-control links where you want to vendor headers only: asio and struct_pack ship in thirdparty/, so there is no brpc/protobuf/gflags dependency stack to build.
Simple server-to-client notifications, using the built-in topic publish/subscribe.
when_not_to_use: Across untrusted networks. Master has no TLS ('support ssl' is an unchecked TODO in C++20 rewrite PR #169) and no authentication, and the server allocates whatever uint64 `body_len` a request header claims, with no size cap.
Polyglot or interop setups. It is C++-only with a custom protocol and speaks neither gRPC nor brpc (a Python-support request, #158, is still open).

Many concurrent requests on one connection. Master runs one call at a time per connection: the client writes, then waits for the reply, and the server reads, runs the handler, writes, then reads again. A slow handler therefore blocks later calls on that connection, and sequence-number multiplexing exists only in unmerged PR #177.
Production-RPC needs such as load balancing, a client connection pool (also a TODO in #169), streaming (unmerged stream_api PR #173), service discovery or metrics.
If you picked it for the published speedup: those numbers are for the retired C++11 code (msgpack, future-based client), not current master. Master also needs GCC 12+, Clang 15+ or MSVC 2022.

integration.dependencies: standalone asio 1.36.0 and the yalantinglibs struct_pack/reflection headers (both vendored under thirdparty/); a threads library
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; GCC 12+, Clang 15+, MSVC 2022 per the README
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (CI runs Ubuntu gcc/clang, macOS clang, and Windows MSVC in Debug only); architecture not restricted by the code. The wire header is host-endian unless both sides call enable_cross_ending(true).
integration.thread_safety: Server: one io_context per thread and a mutex-guarded connection map. Handlers for different connections run concurrently, so shared handler state needs your own locking. Client: each rpc_client owns one socket and one receive buffer and runs on a lazily started global io_context pool (hardware_concurrency threads). It supports one outstanding call at a time; concurrent calls on one client are not documented, so use one client per concurrent caller, as tests/bench.cpp does.

gotchas: A lone numeric argument or return value is sent as text: std::to_string going out, std::from_chars coming back (codec.h). Under C++20, a single double is therefore rounded to 6 decimal places (1e-9 arrives as 0). Multi-argument calls and structs use binary struct_pack.
A timed-out call (`call_for`; plain `call` defaults to 5 s) makes the watchdog close the socket, so every later call on that client fails until you reconnect.

The client decodes the response body as the declared return type even when the server reports an error such as no_such_function or function_exception. For non-string return types the error text fails to parse, so `co_await call` throws std::invalid_argument instead of returning `r.ec`. This comes from reading rpc_client.hpp; tests cover these error paths only at the router level.

Function ids are 32-bit MD5 hashes of the compiler-derived qualified name (__PRETTY_FUNCTION__/__FUNCSIG__). Both sides must declare the function with the same name and namespace, and a duplicate or colliding id throws std::invalid_argument at registration. Whether ids match across different compilers is not documented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rest_rpc over brpc or SRPC when both ends are C++20 code you control and you want header-only, IDL-free function registration with nothing to build. Pick brpc (single/pooled/short connections, load balancers, protobuf services) or SRPC (SRPC/bRPC/Thrift/tRPC protocols, protobuf/Thrift IDL, HTTP+JSON, OpenTelemetry tracing) for production multi-service systems, and grpcxx when clients must speak standard gRPC.
verified_claims_summary: A 2019 first-party doc on the cpp11 branch tested the old C++11 rest_rpc against Apache brpc with echoes of 1K-64K strings, client and server on one i5-9400F 6-core machine (Ubuntu 18.04, g++ 8.2.0, CMake Release). With a single-thread client rest_rpc got 52,631 vs 41,667 QPS at 1K (~1.26x) and 16,949 vs 8,982 at 64K (~1.89x); with 6-20 client threads, in an undefined 'high-efficiency mode', it was 1.19-1.93x. Elapsed time was measured in whole seconds (200,000 QPS works out to 600,000 calls in 3 s), the benchmark code exists only as partial snippets, current master has no comparative numbers, and the README's 'far exceeds gRPC' was never measured.
status_note: Active (master last commit 2026-06-23; multiplexing PR #177 opened 2026-09-03), MIT-licensed and header-only, so easy to vendor. The October 2025 C++20 rewrite (PR #169) changed the API and dropped SSL, so treat master as young code.
